The answer combines convenience and resource control rather than reducing the OS to one application or device function.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Internet access is one supported communication activity rather than the general purpose of an operating system.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Document and spreadsheet creation are application tasks that use OS services rather than define the OS.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Designing hardware is not the runtime resource/service function described for an operating system.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The OS provides interfaces and controlled resource services linking users/programs to the underlying hardware.

evidence.quote: An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs. Convenience means making tasks easy through consistent interfaces, files and device abstractions. Efficiency means using resources effectively; it is not synonymous with the fastest response for every process. Application development tools use OS services but application development itself is not a core resource-management function.

questions.stem:
A user installs a new printer. The OS automatically detects and configures it. This is an 
example of:
questions.hint: Separate device hardware, device-specific software and general event or transfer mechanisms.

answer.text: Plug-and-play functionality.
answer.explanation: OS34 defines plug-and-play as discovering/configuring compatible new hardware, which directly matches automatic printer setup. A driver may still be needed, so automatic configuration does not imply driver-free operation. Manual driver installation and hardware management contradict the scenario’s automatic action. Resource allocation may occur during setup but is broader than the specific feature named.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Automatic detection and configuration of the printer is the note’s plug-and-play behavior.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The stem specifies automatic setup, not user-performed manual installation of a driver.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Manual hardware management does not match the automatic discovery/configuration described in the scenario.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Allocation can be part of setup, but it does not specifically name automatic device discovery/configuration.

evidence.quote: Plug-and-play discovers/configures compatible new hardware but may still require a driver.

questions.stem:
In a system, resources cannot be forcibly taken from processes; they must be released 
voluntarily. Which deadlock condition does this represent?
questions.hint: Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock.

answer.text: No preemption.
answer.explanation: OS22 defines no resource preemption as voluntary release by the current holder. The stem repeats that resources cannot be forcibly taken, giving a direct match. Holding while requesting another resource, one-at-a-time ownership and a closed chain of waits are separate conditions and do not by themselves express the withdrawal restriction.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The holder must release voluntarily, so the system cannot forcibly preempt the resource.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hold-and-wait concerns retaining one resource while requesting another rather than whether withdrawal is allowed.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Mutual exclusion limits simultaneous ownership, not whether allocated resources can be forcibly reclaimed.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Circular wait concerns a closed dependency chain, not the resource-release rule specified here.

evidence.quote: Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another. No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.

questions.stem: How does an operating system improve efficiency in a multi-user environment?

options.label: A
options.text: By allowing only one user to access the system at a time

options.label: C
options.text:
By using time-sharing and process scheduling to allocate CPU time fairly among 
users and processes

options.label: D
options.text: By requiring manual intervention for each task

questions.hint: Compare interaction, CPU sharing and deadline requirements under the stated system model.

answer.text: Time-sharing and scheduling distribute CPU service among users/processes.
answer.explanation: OS02 describes time-sharing as rapid scheduling/preemption supporting interactive users. OS20 explains that fair allocation needs a share policy and may operate per user/group. C describes those relevant mechanisms rather than disabling services or requiring manual intervention. Its fairly should be understood under a specified policy, not as an automatic equality guarantee from time-sharing alone.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Restricting access to one user contradicts the multiuser setting rather than explaining its efficient sharing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Disabling every background service is neither required nor the time-sharing/resource-allocation mechanism described.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Scheduling/time-sharing interleave useful work and can allocate service according to the system’s fairness policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Manual intervention for each task adds administration rather than explaining efficient automatic CPU allocation.

evidence.quote: Multiprogramming keeps several jobs available so another can use the CPU while one waits; it does not require fixed time slices. Time-sharing uses rapid scheduling/preemption to support interactive users. A single CPU interleaves execution; multiple CPUs can execute work truly in parallel.

Fair-share scheduling allocates according to stated weights, potentially per user/group rather than per process. Equal per-process RR can let a user obtain more aggregate CPU by launching more processes. Proportional shares address that policy choice; fair need not mean equal.

questions.stem: What is the primary role of an Operating System?

options.label: B
options.text: Manage hardware and software resources and act as interface between user and hardware

questions.hint: Separate broad resource-management goals from individual services or applications.

answer.text: Manage resources and provide interfaces/services.
answer.explanation: OS01 defines both allocation of CPU/memory/storage/devices/communications and services to programs, while describing convenient interfaces. B combines those core responsibilities. Running applications only, providing connectivity only or permanently storing files each captures a narrower task and omits the overall system-management role. The primary role is therefore the resource/interface combination, not a single service.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Application execution is supported, but only excludes the OS’s other essential resource and service duties.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Resource management plus user/program interfaces matches the combined OS role defined here.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Internet connectivity is one communication service rather than the complete primary OS role.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Permanent file storage is a storage-device/filesystem service and not the complete operating-system purpose.

evidence.quote: An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs. Convenience means making tasks easy through consistent interfaces, files and device abstractions. Efficiency means using resources effectively; it is not synonymous with the fastest response for every process. Application development tools use OS services but application development itself is not a core resource-management function.

questions.stem: Which type of OS is designed to process large numbers of similar jobs without user interaction during execution?
questions.hint: Compare interaction, CPU sharing and deadline requirements under the stated system model.

answer.text: Batch system.
answer.explanation: OS02 defines batch jobs as running with little interaction after submission. That matches processing submitted similar jobs without user interaction during execution. Time-sharing targets interactive users, real-time targets timing correctness, and single-user classifies concurrent access rather than job interaction. The job-processing clue therefore selects batch rather than a user-count or deadline category.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Real-time classification concerns meeting deadlines rather than the absence of user interaction during submitted job processing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Time-sharing supports interactive users through rapid scheduling, unlike the noninteractive batch description.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Batch processing runs submitted jobs with little interaction, directly matching the scenario.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Single-user describes concurrent user access, not whether a workload is submitted and processed as batches.

evidence.quote: Batch jobs run with little interaction after submission. Multiprogramming keeps several jobs available so another can use the CPU while one waits; it does not require fixed time slices. Time-sharing uses rapid scheduling/preemption to support interactive users.

Single-user and multiuser describe concurrent user access, not the number of applications. Network systems expose remote services; distributed systems coordinate work across machines, sometimes hiding location. Real-time correctness includes timing: hard deadlines must be met, while soft deadline misses degrade service.

questions.stem: In a Process Control Block (PCB), what does the Program Counter store?

options.label: B
options.text: The address of the next instruction to be executed for that process

options.label: C
options.text: The amount of CPU time used

questions.hint: Distinguish stored instructions, an executing instance and its saved execution state.

answer.text: The saved next-instruction position for resuming the process.
answer.explanation: OS05 says the PCB records PC/registers alongside scheduling, memory/accounting and I/O information, and a saved PC identifies where execution resumes. Thus B describes its specific field role. Priority, CPU usage and open files can be other PCB information, but they are not the program-counter value. The question requires distinguishing fields within one record rather than excluding them from the PCB entirely.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Priority is scheduling information in the PCB, not the saved next-instruction position held by PC.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The saved PC records the instruction position at which the process will resume execution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: CPU time consumed is accounting information rather than the program-counter address.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Open files belong to I/O/open-resource state, not to the saved instruction-pointer field.

evidence.quote: A saved PC identifies where execution resumes.

questions.stem: Which process state indicates that a process is waiting for an I/O event to complete?
questions.hint: Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role.

answer.text: Waiting/blocked.
answer.explanation: OS06 defines waiting/blocked as unable to proceed until an event and maps blocking I/O from running to waiting. Therefore a process waiting for I/O completion is in Waiting. It is not ready while the event prevents progress, not running during the wait, and not terminated merely because its request is outstanding. Completion normally makes it ready afterward.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ready means eligible for CPU immediately; the outstanding blocking I/O prevents that eligibility.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Running means currently using a CPU, unlike the blocked interval awaiting I/O completion.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Waiting/blocked is the state for a process that cannot proceed until its I/O event completes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Terminated means execution has ended, not temporarily paused pending completion of an I/O request.

evidence.quote: New processes are created/admitted; ready means eligible for CPU but not currently running. Running uses a CPU. Waiting/blocked means unable to proceed until an event; terminated means execution has ended. Running→ready follows time-slice expiry or another preemption. Running→waiting follows blocking I/O. I/O completion normally gives waiting→ready, not a guaranteed immediate running state.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of a Context Switch?

options.label: B
options.text: To save the state of the current process and restore the state of the next scheduled process

options.label: C
options.text: To allocate more memory to a process

questions.hint: Distinguish stored instructions, an executing instance and its saved execution state.

answer.text: Save one execution context and restore another.
answer.explanation: OS05 directly defines a context switch as saving one execution context and restoring another, with overhead interrupting useful application work. B matches. A process may later resume, so switching does not permanently stop or kill it. Allocating memory is another management operation, and a privilege transition alone need not switch processes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The outgoing process can resume later; permanent stopping is termination rather than context switching.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Saving current state and restoring the selected execution context is the defined context-switch purpose.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Memory allocation changes resource assignment, not the saved/restored execution context defining a switch.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A context switch need not terminate any process, regardless of priority.

evidence.quote: A context switch saves one execution context and restores another; useful application work is interrupted by this overhead. An interrupt or system call can switch privilege without switching process.

questions.stem: Which scheduler is responsible for selecting which process from the ready queue should be executed next on the CPU?
questions.hint: Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role.

answer.text: Short-term (CPU) scheduler.
answer.explanation: OS06 assigns admission to the long-term scheduler, suspension/swapping to the medium-term scheduler and ready-work selection to the short-term scheduler. The question specifically asks which ready process receives the CPU next, so C is exact. The dispatcher then performs the handoff; that is distinct from selecting the ready process. Device request ordering is not CPU ready-queue selection.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The long-term scheduler admits jobs rather than making each immediate ready-queue CPU selection.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The medium-term scheduler suspends/swaps work rather than choosing the next CPU-ready process.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The short-term CPU scheduler selects the next eligible process from ready work.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An I/O scheduler orders device work rather than selecting the next process for the CPU.

evidence.quote: The ready queue contains eligible work; device queues hold blocked requests. The broad textbook job queue contains processes in the system, while an admission queue more narrowly holds jobs awaiting memory/admission. Long-term scheduling admits jobs; medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work. The dispatcher performs the handoff/context restore after selection.

questions.stem: What is the role of the Medium-Term Scheduler?

options.label: A
options.text: Decide which jobs enter the system

options.label: B
options.text: Pick the next process for the CPU

options.label: C
options.text: Swap processes between main memory and secondary storage to manage memory

questions.hint: Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role.

answer.text: Suspend/swap processes between resident and backing-store states.
answer.explanation: OS06 explicitly assigns suspension/swapping to the medium-term scheduler. OS27 distinguishes traditional whole-process swapping to backing storage from page movement. Thus C is the matching memory/load-control role. Admitting jobs belongs to long-term scheduling, picking the next ready process to short-term scheduling, and servicing drivers to device-management paths.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Deciding admission into the system is the long-term scheduler’s role in the supplied model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Selecting the next CPU process belongs to the short-term scheduler, not the medium-term one.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps processes to control resident load and memory use.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Device-driver requests concern I/O service rather than the scheduler’s suspension/swapping function.

evidence.quote: Long-term scheduling admits jobs; medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work.
Swapping traditionally moves a whole process to backing store; paging moves individual pages.
A driver converts OS requests into device-specific operations.

questions.stem: A Race Condition occurs when:

options.label: A
options.text: Two processes finish execution at the same time

options.label: B
options.text: Multiple processes access shared resources simultaneously without proper synchronization, causing unpredictable results

options.label: C
options.text: A high-priority process always runs before a low-priority one

options.label: D
options.text: A process is preempted by the OS scheduler

questions.hint: Identify conflicting shared accesses and the safety or progress property required.

answer.text: Uncoordinated conflicting shared accesses make results depend on interleaving.
answer.explanation: OS10 defines a race by results depending on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses. B is the intended match, with shared access understood to include a conflict such as an update; simultaneous read-only access alone is insufficient. Coincident completion, ordinary priority selection and preemption do not by themselves establish a shared-state race.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two completions at the same time need not involve conflicting shared accesses or interleaving-dependent results.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Unsynchronized conflicting shared accesses can make results depend on execution interleaving, which is the race condition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Priority order alone is a scheduling choice and does not establish a conflicting shared-data race.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Preemption can expose a race but is not itself sufficient without conflicting unprotected accesses.

evidence.quote: A race occurs when results depend on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses.
Two threads read counter=0, each computes 1 and each stores 1. Two increments produce 1 instead of 2. Protecting the entire read-modify-write with one lock prevents that lost update.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a necessary condition for deadlock?
questions.hint: Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock.

answer.text: Preemption is not a necessary condition; no-preemption is.
answer.explanation: OS22 names mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no resource preemption and circular wait as the necessary set. The option Preemption reverses one of those conditions. Therefore C is the exception, while the other three are genuine members. This resource-preemption rule is separate from whether CPU scheduling uses timer preemption.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Mutual exclusion is explicitly one of the four necessary conditions in the standard resource model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hold-and-wait is explicitly necessary: a process retains a resource while requesting another.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The required condition is no-preemption; permitting preemption is not one of the necessary conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Circular wait is explicitly a required closed dependency chain in the standard model.

evidence.quote: Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another. No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.
All four are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model.

questions.stem: All three processes arrive at time 0 and are ready immediately. Their CPU burst times are P1 = 24 ms, P2 = 3 ms and P3 = 3 ms. Using non-preemptive FCFS with tie order P1, P2, P3, and ignoring context-switch overhead, what is the average waiting time?
questions.hint: Follow arrival order, include idle periods and distinguish waiting from completion time.

answer.text: 17 ms.
answer.explanation: FCFS runs P1 from 0 to 24 ms, P2 from 24 to 27 ms, and P3 from 27 to 30 ms. Because every process arrives at 0, their waiting times are 0, 24 and 27 ms. The average is (0+24+27)/3 = 51/3 = 17 ms, so C is correct. The average turnaround is a different quantity: (24+27+30)/3 = 27 ms.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 3 ms is the burst time of P2 or P3, not the average ready-queue wait.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The three waits total 51 ms, so dividing by three cannot give 9 ms.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The waits 0, 24 and 27 ms average to 17 ms.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 27 ms is the average turnaround time in this example, not the average waiting time.

evidence.quote: FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt.

All ready at time 0, tie order P1=24,P2=3,P3=3: schedule 0–24 P1,24–27 P2,27–30 P3. Waiting times 0,24,27 average to 17. Turnarounds 24,27,30 average to 27. If arrivals are not simultaneous, recompute using their actual times.
For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B.

questions.stem: What problem does the 'Aging' technique solve in Priority Scheduling?
questions.hint: Check priority direction, preemption and whether waiting can change effective rank.

answer.text: Starvation of low-priority processes.
answer.explanation: OS17 defines aging as increasing waiting jobs’ effective priority to reduce indefinite postponement under suitable rules/workloads. Thus B names the problem it addresses. It does not remove a deadlock dependency cycle, coordinate conflicting memory updates or consolidate fragmented memory. The result still depends on the priority/aging policy; naming aging alone does not provide an unconditional deadline guarantee.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Aging changes priority rather than breaking the blocked resource dependencies of a deadlock.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Increasing effective priority of waiting low-priority jobs addresses their starvation under sustained higher-priority load.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Races require shared-access synchronization; priority aging is not a mutual-exclusion mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Memory fragmentation concerns allocation layout rather than the priority of waiting CPU jobs.

evidence.quote: Aging increases waiting jobs’ effective priority according to a rule, reducing indefinite postponement when the priority scheme and workload permit. It is not a deadlock cure.
A race occurs when results depend on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses.
Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit. External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation.

questions.stem: Which scheduling algorithm is known as preemptive SJF?
questions.hint: Compare the ready jobs using the stated burst or remaining-time rule.

answer.text: Shortest Remaining Time First.
answer.explanation: OS16 distinguishes non-preemptive SJF/SJN from SRTF, which reconsiders at arrivals and can preempt for shorter remaining work. Therefore SRTF is the preemptive SJF variant. RR uses fixed cyclic turns, FCFS arrival order and generic priority an independently defined ranking. The original burst length and the remaining length must not be confused after a job has executed.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RR selects cyclic quantum turns rather than the shortest remaining CPU work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS follows arrival order and is ordinarily non-preemptive rather than preemptive shortest-job scheduling.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SRTF chooses minimum remaining work and can interrupt a running job for a shorter arrival.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Generic priority scheduling does not specifically rank by remaining burst length and can be either variant.

evidence.quote: Non-preemptive SJF/SJN chooses the shortest next burst among currently ready jobs. SRTF reconsiders on arrivals and selects the shortest remaining work; a shorter newcomer can preempt. Future burst lengths normally need estimates.
RR serves a ready queue cyclically for at most quantum q per turn.
FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt.

questions.stem: In Round Robin scheduling, what is the key challenge?

options.label: B
options.text: Determining the appropriate time quantum length

questions.hint: Trace bounded turns in ready-queue order and include the stated overhead and arrivals.

answer.text: Choose an appropriate time quantum.
answer.explanation: OS18 says a large RR quantum approaches FCFS, while tiny quanta increase context-switch overhead. Selecting q therefore trades responsiveness against overhead, matching B. Priority management, deadlock policy and memory allocation are separate concerns rather than the defining parameter-selection challenge of ordinary Round Robin. The useful quantum depends on workloads and switching cost.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Basic RR uses cyclic ready-queue turns rather than requiring a hierarchy of priority levels.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quantum length controls responsiveness and switching overhead, creating RR’s characteristic tuning tradeoff.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Deadlock avoidance concerns resources and dependencies, not the defining RR quantum parameter.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Memory allocation is a separate management problem rather than the Round Robin selection rule’s main parameter.

evidence.quote: A large quantum approaches FCFS; tiny quanta increase switch overhead.

With n continuously ready jobs, no priority bypass and zero overhead, a just-requeued job waits at most (n−1)q for its next turn. This bounds one interval, not total lifetime waiting when arrivals or blocking are unrestricted. Include context-switch costs if given.

questions.stem: What is a Semaphore?

options.label: C
options.text: A synchronization variable that controls access to shared resources in a multi-process environment

options.label: D
options.text: A type of file allocation method

questions.hint: Track available permits and blocked operations using the stated semaphore model.

answer.text: A synchronization variable with atomic wait and signal operations.
answer.explanation: OS11 defines a semaphore through atomic wait/P/down and signal/V/up operations. Tokens control whether participants can proceed with shared resource work, with binary or counting forms. C identifies that synchronization role. Scheduling, memory-management and file-allocation policies solve different resource-selection/layout problems and do not define semaphore semantics.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A semaphore synchronizes participants; it is not itself a CPU-selection scheduling algorithm.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It controls coordination through permits, rather than choosing memory locations or translation layouts.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Atomic wait/signal on a synchronization variable controls permits for concurrent shared-resource operations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: File allocation chooses storage-block layout; that is separate from semaphore synchronization semantics.

evidence.quote: A semaphore provides atomic wait/P/down and signal/V/up operations. Under the nonnegative-token model, wait consumes one available token or blocks when none is available; signal supplies a token and may wake a waiter. Implementations using negative internal counts encode waiters differently, so state the model. A binary semaphore represents one permit; a counting semaphore tracks several. A mutex normally has ownership rules that a general semaphore lacks.
FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt.
A contiguous allocation gives a process one continuous region.
Contiguous allocation uses consecutive blocks; logical block i is start+i and supports direct access, but growth and external fragmentation are problems.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a Binary Semaphore and a Counting Semaphore?

options.label: B
options.text: Binary semaphores have only two states (0 or 1), while counting semaphores track available resources up to a maximum count

options.label: C
options.text: Counting semaphores are used only for deadlock prevention

questions.hint: Track available permits and blocked operations using the stated semaphore model.

answer.text: Binary tracks one permit; counting tracks several.
answer.explanation: OS11 defines a binary semaphore as one permit and a counting semaphore as several, under the nonnegative-token model. Thus binary availability is 0/1 while a resource pool can have a larger count. B states this logical distinction. Internal negative-waiter encodings are implementation details, not a reason to claim speed guarantees, deadlock-only usage or no difference.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The note gives no universal relative-speed guarantee; permit capacity is the defining distinction.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: In the nonnegative-token model, binary availability is zero/one while counting semaphores track several available permits.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Counting semaphores coordinate resource pools and are not limited to preventing deadlock.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The allowed permit count is a substantive difference explicitly stated here.

evidence.quote: A semaphore provides atomic wait/P/down and signal/V/up operations. Under the nonnegative-token model, wait consumes one available token or blocks when none is available; signal supplies a token and may wake a waiter. Implementations using negative internal counts encode waiters differently, so state the model. A binary semaphore represents one permit; a counting semaphore tracks several. A mutex normally has ownership rules that a general semaphore lacks.

questions.stem: What must hold simultaneously for a deadlock to occur?

options.label: A
options.text: Only Mutual Exclusion and Circular Wait

options.label: B
options.text: Any two of the four conditions

options.label: C
options.text: All four necessary conditions: Mutual Exclusion, Hold-and-Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait

questions.hint: Trace the resource dependencies and distinguish necessary conditions from evidence of an actual deadlock.

answer.text: All four standard necessary conditions.
answer.explanation: OS22 says all four conditions are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model. C names that full set. Any two or a cycle alone does not state the complete conjunction. This is a necessary-condition answer, not an assertion that merely allowing all four policies proves a deadlock already exists in a particular allocation state.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It omits hold-and-wait and no-preemption, both necessary in the stated standard resource model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An arbitrary pair does not supply all four necessary restrictions for the standard deadlock model.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This option lists mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no-preemption and circular wait together.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A cycle alone omits other necessary restrictions; it is not the complete standard condition set.

evidence.quote: Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another. No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.
All four are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model. Their availability as general system policies does not prove a deadlock exists at this instant; inspect actual allocations/requests.

questions.stem: In a Resource Allocation Graph (RAG), what does a cycle with single-instance resources indicate?
questions.hint: Follow request and assignment arrows and check how many instances each resource has.

answer.text: Definite deadlock under single-instance resource assumptions.
answer.explanation: OS23 says a cycle implies deadlock when every resource type has one instance. The stem supplies that decisive assumption, so C follows. With multiple instances a cycle would indicate only a possibility, but importing that different model would ignore the literal question. A graph cycle also says nothing by itself about high CPU utilization.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Potential-only applies to the more general multiple-instance caveat, not the supplied single-instance case.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A cycle in the stated single-instance model establishes deadlock rather than excluding it.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note explicitly gives cycle implies deadlock for a graph with one instance per resource type.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Resource dependency cycles do not measure CPU busy time or establish high processor utilization.

evidence.quote: In a resource-allocation graph, P→R is a request and an instance R→P is an assignment. Follow these directions to form waits. No cycle implies no deadlock; with one instance of every resource type, a cycle implies deadlock. With multiple instances a cycle alone is insufficient: another instance may permit completion. A wait-for graph replaces single-instance resource nodes with P→Q when P waits for Q.

questions.stem: Which deadlock handling method allows deadlock to occur but then recovers from it?
questions.hint: Separate handling before allocation from actions taken after detection, and consider the cost of checking.

answer.text: Deadlock recovery.
answer.explanation: OS26 describes recovery through terminating selected processes or safely reclaiming resources and rolling work back after deadlock is detected. That matches allowing occurrence and then resolving it. Prevention removes a necessary condition, avoidance preserves safety before granting, and ignoring accepts risk without committing to recovery. The complete handling strategy is detection plus recovery; C is the offered recovery component.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Prevention constrains requests so the targeted deadlock class cannot arise rather than accepting occurrence first.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ignoring rare deadlock does not define active detection and subsequent recovery.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Recovery acts on an actual detected deadlock using termination, reclamation or rollback as appropriate.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Avoidance checks safe states before grants rather than deliberately permitting deadlock and then repairing it.

evidence.quote: Detection asks whether the current state is deadlocked. Recovery can terminate selected processes or reclaim safely preemptable resources and roll affected work back to a checkpoint. Termination and rollback are both possible recovery tools; choose according to the resource and process conditions.
Prevention constrains how requests are made.
Avoidance allows requests only if the resulting state remains safe.
Ignoring a sufficiently rare problem is sometimes called the ostrich policy, but real systems still prevent or detect selected deadlocks.

questions.stem: What is Address Binding at 'Load Time'?

options.label: A
options.text: Addresses are fixed by the compiler before execution

options.label: B
options.text: Addresses are determined while the program executes

options.label: C
options.text: Final memory addresses are assigned when the program is loaded into memory (since addresses are unknown at compile time)

options.label: D
options.text: Addresses are stored on the hard disk

questions.hint: Track when an address or library reference is resolved and the direction of translation.

answer.text: Relocate addresses when the program is loaded.
answer.explanation: OS27 defines load-time binding as relocation when placed into memory. That matches C’s final-address assignment at load when placement was unknown at compile time. Fixing absolute addresses during compilation is compile-time binding; translating while running is execution-time binding. Merely storing address bytes on a disk describes neither the placement decision nor its timing.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fixing absolute addresses in the compiler is compile-time binding, not relocation on loading.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Translation during execution is execution-time binding rather than assignment during loading.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The loader resolves placement-dependent addresses when placing the program into memory.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Storing address information on disk does not define when placement-dependent address binding occurs.

evidence.quote: Compile-time binding uses absolute addresses if placement is known. Load-time binding relocates when placed into memory. Execution-time binding translates while running and permits movement with hardware support.

questions.stem: Under basic page-frame allocation and variable-segment allocation, which statement correctly contrasts allocation-unit size and external fragmentation?

options.label: A
options.text: Paging uses variable-sized blocks; segmentation uses fixed-sized blocks

options.label: B
options.text: Paging divides memory into fixed-sized pages eliminating external fragmentation; segmentation uses variable-sized logical segments but can cause external fragmentation

options.label: C
options.text: Segmentation is used only in virtual memory

questions.hint: Check the logical region and offset bound before computing its physical location.

answer.text: Fixed-size paging avoids external page-frame fragmentation; variable segments can fragment externally.
answer.explanation: Paging maps fixed-size pages into equal-size frames, avoiding external fragmentation of frame allocation, although internal waste can remain. Segmentation uses variable-length logical regions and can leave external holes. This is the unit-size and fragmentation contrast in B. A reverses the sizes. C does not supply that contrast, and D substitutes a hardware-support claim for it; page translation still requires mappings and checks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The sizes are reversed: pages are fixed-size units and segments are variable-length regions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This gives the required fixed-page versus variable-segment size and external-fragmentation contrast.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An exclusive-use statement does not compare allocation-unit sizes or external fragmentation as requested.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This does not give the requested size/fragmentation contrast; paging also uses translation mappings and checks.

evidence.quote: Under the basic models, paging uses fixed units/page tables and can waste space internally; segmentation uses variable logical units/segment tables and can fragment externally. Segments reflect program structure whereas ordinary pages are largely transparent to applications.

Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P. Divide virtual address v into page=floor(v/P) and offset=v mod P. The page table maps a page to a frame and protection/status flags. Physical address=frame×P+offset.

questions.stem: What causes External Fragmentation in memory management?

options.label: A
options.text: Allocated memory blocks being larger than needed

options.label: B
options.text: Free memory being scattered in small non-contiguous pieces making it impossible to satisfy large allocation requests

options.label: C
options.text: Processes using too much CPU time

options.label: D
options.text: Too many open files in the directory

questions.hint: Locate unused space relative to an allocated unit and distinguish total free space from contiguous free space.

answer.text: Free capacity is split across holes too small for a required contiguous allocation.
answer.explanation: OS29 defines external fragmentation as sufficient total free space split into holes unable to satisfy a contiguous allocation. B matches that definition, with large requests understood to require one continuous region. A instead describes internal fragmentation. CPU time and open-file counts may create other pressures but do not define the spatial fragmentation of free memory.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Unused space within an oversized allocated block is internal fragmentation, not external free-hole fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Noncontiguous small holes can have enough total capacity yet fail to satisfy one contiguous request.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: CPU execution time does not define the spatial layout of free memory holes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Open-file count is a resource-use limit rather than the definition of external memory fragmentation.

evidence.quote: Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit. External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the Page Table in Paging?

options.label: A
options.text: To allocate CPU time to processes

options.label: B
options.text: To map logical page numbers to physical frame numbers in memory

questions.hint: Split the address into page and offset, then apply the mapping and access checks.

answer.text: Map virtual/logical pages to physical frames.
answer.explanation: OS30 says the page table maps each virtual page to a frame with protection/status flags. B directly states the primary translation role. CPU time allocation belongs to scheduling; file permissions belong to filesystem metadata, despite page tables also having memory-protection bits. Disk I/O may service nonresident pages but does not define the page table’s mapping purpose.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU time allocation is scheduling, not the page-to-frame translation recorded by a page table.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The table identifies the physical frame corresponding to each virtual page and records relevant flags.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Memory access-protection flags differ from filesystem file-access permissions; file permissions are not the page table’s purpose.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Page faults may cause I/O, but general disk-operation management is not the table’s translation role.

evidence.quote: Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P. Divide virtual address v into page=floor(v/P) and offset=v mod P. The page table maps a page to a frame and protection/status flags.

A file has content and metadata such as name, size, owner, permissions and timestamps. open obtains an open-file reference, read/write transfer bytes, seek changes an offset, close releases a reference, truncate changes size and unlink removes a name.

questions.stem: In Segmentation, how is a physical address calculated?
questions.hint: Check the logical region and offset bound before computing its physical location.

answer.text: Physical address = segment base + valid offset.
answer.explanation: OS31 gives segment-table base, limit and permissions, then validates (segment,offset) and adds base+offset. B matches, conditional on the offset passing the bound/protection checks. A and D mix in paging components and omit required scaling or displacement, while subtracting a limit is not the segment translation formula. An invalid offset traps rather than spilling into another segment.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Page number times frame size is not the segment base-plus-offset translation and omits required mapping.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: After segment and bound checks, add the selected segment’s physical base to the offset.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The limit is a bound for validation, not a number subtracted to form the physical address.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Frame terminology belongs to paging, and adding an unscaled frame number is not the segmentation formula.

evidence.quote: Segmentation uses logical variable-length units such as code, stack and arrays. A segment-table entry provides base, limit and permissions. For (segment,offset), validate the segment and check the bound, then add base+offset. An out-of-range offset traps; it must not spill into the next segment.

Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P. Divide virtual address v into page=floor(v/P) and offset=v mod P. The page table maps a page to a frame and protection/status flags. Physical address=frame×P+offset.

questions.stem: What is Virtual Memory?

options.label: A
options.text: Extra RAM chips added to a computer

options.label: B
options.text: A technique using hard disk space as an extension of physical memory, allowing programs larger than physical memory to execute

options.label: C
options.text: The memory inside the CPU cache

options.label: D
options.text: Memory used only by the operating system

questions.hint: Separate a permitted nonresident access from an illegal access and trace the required handling steps.

answer.text: Translated protected address spaces can use backing storage for nonresident portions.
answer.explanation: OS32 describes virtual memory as protected translated address spaces with nonresident program portions backed by storage. B gives the disk-backed extension aspect and can allow programs exceeding resident physical memory to execute. It is not a complete definition of virtual memory, nor does it eliminate finite capacity constraints. The other alternatives confuse RAM installation, cache or an OS-only restriction.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Installing RAM chips adds physical capacity; virtual-memory translation is a different mechanism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Backing storage holds nonresident portions, permitting a program’s address space to exceed its currently resident physical memory.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: CPU cache retains copied memory blocks and is not the virtual-address/backing-store mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Processes receive virtual address spaces; virtual memory is not restricted to storage used only by the OS.

evidence.quote: Virtual memory provides translated, protected address spaces and allows nonresident portions of a program to be backed by storage. It does not add physical RAM or remove all capacity constraints.
Caching retains copies to accelerate reuse.

questions.stem: In demand paging, assume the accessed virtual page is valid, permitted and backed by disk, but its contents are not resident and must be read from disk. What event is the page fault in this scenario?

options.label: B
options.text: When the CPU tries to access a page not currently in physical memory, requiring the OS to load it from disk

options.label: C
options.text: An error in the page table

options.label: D
options.text: When a process exceeds its allocated memory

questions.hint: Separate a permitted nonresident access from an illegal access and trace the required handling steps.

answer.text: When the CPU tries to access a page not currently in physical memory, requiring the OS to load it from disk
answer.explanation: A valid nonresident access traps so the OS can obtain the page contents, update the mapping and restart the access. The specified page is disk-backed and requires a read, making B accurate for this scenario. Page faults in general need not read disk; zero-fill and shared mappings are other cases. Nothing here requires hardware failure, table corruption or exceeding the permitted address range.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The trap does not imply damaged memory hardware.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The valid disk-backed page is nonresident, so this access requires the stated page-in.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A correct table may intentionally mark a valid page nonresident.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The page is explicitly within the valid permitted mapping, so no allocation violation is implied.

evidence.quote: Demand paging brings a page in when accessed. On a nonresident access: trap, validate mapping/permissions, find a frame or choose a victim, save a dirty victim if needed, obtain contents, update mapping and restart.
Not every fault reads a disk: some allocate zero-filled pages or establish shared mappings. An illegal access is rejected, not automatically loaded.

questions.stem: What is Demand Paging?

options.label: A
options.text: Loading the entire program into memory before execution

options.label: B
options.text: Loading only the pages that are actually needed during program execution, keeping others on disk until required

options.label: D
options.text: Swapping entire processes between memory and disk

questions.hint: Separate a permitted nonresident access from an illegal access and trace the required handling steps.

answer.text: Bring a page into memory when it is needed/accessed.
answer.explanation: OS32 defines demand paging as bringing a page in when accessed. B matches loading only the pages demanded during execution, with disk backing for the described stored portions. Not all pages must literally originate on disk because zero-fill/shared cases exist. Whole-program loading, fixed contiguous partitions and whole-process swapping do not name this per-page demand policy.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Loading the entire program before execution is eager loading rather than fetching pages on demand.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Pages are brought in as execution needs them; disk backing is the described common stored-page case.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fixed partitions are a contiguous-allocation arrangement rather than the page-access-triggered loading policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Moving an entire process is traditional swapping, not the individual-page demand mechanism.

evidence.quote: Demand paging brings a page in when accessed. On a nonresident access: trap, validate mapping/permissions, find a frame or choose a victim, save a dirty victim if needed, obtain contents, update mapping and restart.
Swapping traditionally moves a whole process to backing store; paging moves individual pages.
A contiguous allocation gives a process one continuous region.

questions.stem: What is the difference between Internal and External Fragmentation?

options.label: A
options.text: Both are the same type of memory waste

options.label: B
options.text: Internal fragmentation wastes space inside allocated partitions (allocated > needed); external fragmentation wastes space between allocations

options.label: C
options.text: External fragmentation occurs in paging systems

options.label: D
options.text: Internal fragmentation only occurs in virtual memory

questions.hint: Locate unused space relative to an allocated unit and distinguish total free space from contiguous free space.

answer.text: Internal waste is inside allocations; external holes are between them.
answer.explanation: OS29 defines internal fragmentation as unused space inside an allocated unit and external fragmentation as free holes unable to serve a required contiguous request. B states the location distinction. C is not the general definition and needs allocator scope; D adds an unsupported virtual-memory-only restriction. These wastes can arise from allocation geometry rather than the program’s CPU behavior.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The note explicitly distinguishes internal unused allocation space from external free-hole fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Internal space is wasted within an allocation; external waste is free space split between allocations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This does not define the contrast; basic page-frame allocation avoids external fragmentation, though other allocators may differ.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Unused space within an allocated unit is not limited by definition to virtual-memory systems.

evidence.quote: Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit. External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation.
Basic fixed-frame paging avoids external fragmentation of page-frame allocation but can waste the final page internally.

questions.stem: Which memory allocation strategy picks the first hole large enough to accommodate a process?
questions.hint: Apply the stated hole-selection or base-and-bound rule with its explicit convention.

answer.text: First-fit.
answer.explanation: OS28 defines first-fit as selecting the first adequate hole. This is exactly the stem’s first hole large enough. Best-fit searches for the smallest adequate hole, worst-fit for the largest, and next-fit resumes from a prior search position. The explicit first-hole condition selects first-fit without any numeric hole trace.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Best-fit minimizes adequate hole size rather than stopping at the first adequate hole.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Worst-fit selects the largest available hole rather than the first adequate one encountered.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: First-fit stops at the first hole that can accommodate the requested allocation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Next-fit continues from the previous search position; the stem gives the ordinary first-fit criterion.

evidence.quote: First-fit selects the first adequate hole; next-fit continues from the previous search position; best-fit selects the smallest adequate hole; worst-fit selects the largest.

questions.stem: What is Swapping in OS memory management?

options.label: B
options.text: Temporarily moving an entire process from main memory to a backing store (disk) to free memory for other processes

options.label: D
options.text: Replacing old CPU instructions with new ones

questions.hint: Track when an address or library reference is resolved and the direction of translation.

answer.text: Temporarily move a whole process to backing store.
answer.explanation: OS27 explicitly distinguishes traditional swapping of a whole process to backing store from paging individual pages and context switching execution state. B describes the whole-process memory-management operation. Saving registers is a context-switch task, file copying is a filesystem operation, and replacing instruction contents does not define swapping’s residence change.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Saving/restoring CPU register contexts is context switching rather than moving a whole process out of RAM.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Traditional swapping moves a process image to backing storage to free resident memory.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Copying files changes directory/storage contents rather than a process image’s memory residence.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Replacing instruction contents is not the defined transfer of a whole process between RAM and backing store.

evidence.quote: Swapping traditionally moves a whole process to backing store; paging moves individual pages. These differ from a context switch, which primarily changes execution state.
A context switch saves one execution context and restores another; useful application work is interrupted by this overhead.

questions.stem: What is Dynamic Loading?

options.label: A
options.text: Loading the entire program into memory at startup

options.label: B
options.text: Loading routines from disk into memory only when they are actually called during execution

options.label: C
options.text: Dynamically changing the priority of a process

options.label: D
options.text: Moving pages between RAM and disk automatically

questions.hint: Track when an address or library reference is resolved and the direction of translation.

answer.text: Load a routine only when needed.
answer.explanation: OS27 directly defines dynamic loading as bringing a routine in when needed. B states the routine-on-call form of that rule. Eager startup loading is the opposite, priority changes are scheduling, and automatic page movement is a virtual-memory mechanism at a different granularity. Dynamic loading concerns when code routines become resident, not which process gets CPU priority.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Loading all routines at startup is eager loading rather than bringing them in only on demand.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A routine is loaded when execution actually calls or needs it, matching dynamic loading.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Changing priority affects scheduling and does not load a routine’s code into memory.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Paging moves pages by virtual-memory demand, whereas dynamic loading names demand-driven routine loading.

evidence.quote: Dynamic loading brings a routine in when needed.
Demand paging brings a page in when accessed.
Priority scheduling chooses the highest-priority ready job.

questions.stem: What is the key management-layer distinction between user-level threads and kernel-level threads, without assuming universal speed or reliability advantages?

options.label: A
options.text: User-level threads are managed by a user-space library; kernel-level threads are known to and managed by the OS

options.label: C
options.text: User-level threads can access hardware directly

options.label: D
options.text: There is no practical difference between them

questions.hint: Compare per-thread execution context with shared process resources and the stated thread mapping.

answer.text: User-level threads are managed by a user-space library; kernel-level threads are known to and managed by the OS
answer.explanation: User-level threads are managed by a library, while kernel threads are execution contexts known to the OS. Their mapping affects blocking behavior and use of multiple CPUs. The management layer alone does not guarantee faster creation, faster execution or greater stability; those depend on implementation. It also does not grant user code privileged hardware access. The option keeps the supported management distinction.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This states library management versus OS-known kernel threads.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: No management layer guarantees that kernel threads are always faster.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: User-level thread management does not grant direct privileged hardware access.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Blocking and CPU-use differences show that the distinction has practical effects.

evidence.quote: User-level threads are managed by a library; kernel threads are known to the OS. In many-to-one mapping, a blocking kernel call can block all user threads and one kernel execution context cannot use multiple CPUs simultaneously. One-to-one permits another kernel thread to run when one blocks. Many-to-many multiplexes user threads over several kernel threads. Speed and reliability depend on implementation; the management layer alone guarantees neither. Application names such as browser or Excel do not prove a particular version’s threading model.

Being scheduled or managed by the kernel does not give application thread code kernel privilege. Ordinary applications and supporting utilities execute in restricted user mode and request protected services through libraries and system calls. Kernel component code executes in privileged kernel mode and performs permitted low-level hardware operations.

questions.stem: What is IPC (Inter-Process Communication)?

options.label: B
options.text: Mechanisms allowing processes to exchange information, synchronize, and coordinate activities

options.label: C
options.text: A method for allocating memory between processes

questions.hint: Identify how data moves, which participant waits and what event allows the operation to continue.

answer.text: Mechanisms for exchanging information and coordinating processes.
answer.explanation: OS09 describes shared-memory communication, send/receive, pipes, queues, sockets and RPC, including synchronization for conflicting updates. B summarizes the exchange and coordination role. IPC is not a CPU selection algorithm or a particular memory-allocation/file operation, even though shared memory and file-based mechanisms may be used to implement it.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU scheduling selects execution opportunities, rather than defining communication and coordination among processes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Exchanging information with appropriate synchronization/coordination captures the IPC mechanisms described here.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shared memory can implement IPC, but memory allocation alone does not define interprocess communication.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Files can participate in communication, but IPC is not restricted to one filesystem operation.

evidence.quote: Shared memory lets processes access a common region and requires synchronization for conflicting updates. Message passing exchanges data through send/receive operations. Pipes provide streams; message queues preserve messages; sockets connect endpoints; RPC requests a remote operation. HTTP is an application protocol over a communication mechanism and can carry interprocess communication, so it is not universally “not IPC.”
File locks coordinate access rather than transfer arbitrary payloads, though locking is synchronization within IPC.

questions.stem: What is the Critical Section problem concerned with?

options.label: A
options.text: Preventing processes from using too much CPU

options.label: B
options.text: Ensuring that no two processes are executing their critical sections (code accessing shared resources) simultaneously

questions.hint: Identify conflicting shared accesses and the safety or progress property required.

answer.text: Mutually exclude conflicting critical-region execution.
answer.explanation: OS10 defines a critical section as code accessing shared state needing protection and lists mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting as requirements. B states the exclusion aspect for critical sections protecting the same conflicting resource. The problem also includes progress/fair-waiting requirements, so exclusion is not its entire specification. CPU quotas, disk management and real-time scheduling are different topics.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU consumption limits are not the shared-access exclusion problem defining critical sections.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Conflicting critical regions must not execute simultaneously; this is the mutual-exclusion part of the correctness requirements.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Disk I/O can involve shared state, but managing it generally is not the critical-section problem definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Real-time selection addresses timing/scheduling, not the core shared-state exclusion requirement requested.

evidence.quote: A race occurs when results depend on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses. A critical section is code accessing shared state that needs protection, not the resource itself. A correct exclusion solution requires mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting under stated assumptions. Mutual exclusion is a desired safety property; races, starvation and deadlock are possible failures.

Keep critical regions small and ensure every conflicting access uses the same protection. A barrier waits until a defined set of participants reaches a point; a monitor encapsulates protected operations with condition synchronization. Locking can itself introduce deadlock if acquisition order is inconsistent.

questions.stem: For a general process that may perform I/O, which formula defines turnaround time from event timestamps? Waiting means time in the ready queue; burst means total CPU service. The formula must remain valid for nonzero arrival times and blocked intervals.
questions.hint: Construct a timeline and distinguish completion rates from individual elapsed-time measures.

answer.text: Completion Time - Arrival Time
answer.explanation: Turnaround is completion time minus arrival time, including CPU execution, ready-queue waiting and blocked intervals. Ready waiting plus CPU service omits blocked time when I/O occurs. Start plus burst may resemble a completion timestamp for uninterrupted work, but it is not elapsed turnaround and does not subtract arrival. Burst minus waiting has no general elapsed-time interpretation. Only B remains valid in the full stated model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Subtracting ready waiting from CPU service is not turnaround.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Completion minus arrival includes the entire elapsed lifetime.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Start plus burst is not generally completion with I/O and does not subtract arrival.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Ready waiting plus CPU service omits blocked intervals.

evidence.quote: For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B. With I/O, subtract all CPU and blocked time to isolate ready-queue waiting.

questions.stem: What is the Convoy Effect in FCFS scheduling?

options.label: B
options.text: All processes receive equal CPU time

options.label: C
options.text: Short processes get stuck waiting behind one very long process, causing high average waiting times

options.label: D
options.text: Multiple processes share the same memory space

questions.hint: Follow arrival order, include idle periods and distinguish waiting from completion time.

answer.text: Short jobs wait behind a long FCFS burst.
answer.explanation: OS15 describes the convoy effect as long CPU-bound work making many short jobs wait under non-preemptive FCFS. C directly states that queueing effect and its high waiting-time consequence. FCFS does not use priority order or grant equal total CPU, and shared address space is unrelated to the arrival-order delay. The effect depends on a long burst preceding shorter ones.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Priority order does not define FCFS, which follows arrival order rather than high-priority completion.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS serves entire bursts of possibly different lengths rather than enforcing equal CPU shares.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Short jobs are delayed behind the long non-preempted burst, producing the FCFS convoy effect.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shared memory concerns address-space organization rather than the scheduling delay called a convoy.

evidence.quote: FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt. If the CPU is idle, jump to the next arrival. Long CPU-bound work can make many short jobs wait: the convoy effect.
RR gives recurring opportunities, not identical total CPU consumption for jobs of different lengths.
A thread has its own PC, registers and stack. Threads in a process share code, address space and usually open-file resources.

questions.stem: What is Cooperative (Non-Preemptive) vs Preemptive Scheduling?

options.label: B
options.text: Non-preemptive: process runs until it voluntarily releases CPU; Preemptive: OS can forcibly take CPU from a running process for another

options.label: D
options.text: Non-preemptive scheduling always gives better performance

questions.hint: Check whether the running burst can be interrupted before completion or blocking.

answer.text: Voluntary release versus possible forced CPU preemption.
answer.explanation: OS14 says non-preemptive scheduling retains the CPU until completion, blocking or voluntary yielding, while preemptive scheduling may return running work to ready. B captures the voluntary-versus-forced distinction, with completion/blocking included among natural release events. C contradicts preemption, D claims an unsupported universal performance ranking, and A erases the defining difference.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The policies differ in whether a running CPU burst can be forcibly interrupted for another process.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Non-preemptive work releases naturally/voluntarily; preemptive policy may forcibly reassign CPU execution time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Forcibly interrupting running work is exactly what preemptive scheduling permits.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No policy universally performs better for all workloads and objectives, so the absolute performance claim fails.

evidence.quote: Non-preemptive scheduling keeps a running CPU burst until completion, blocking or voluntary yielding. Preemptive scheduling can return running work to ready, usually after a timer quantum or a more urgent arrival. FCFS and non-preemptive SJF are non-preemptive; RR and SRTF are preemptive. Priority can be either, so its name alone cannot decide. Cooperative describes relying on voluntary release.
There is no universally best policy for response, waiting, fairness and throughput simultaneously.

questions.stem: Which scheduling criterion measures the number of processes completed per unit of time?
questions.hint: Construct a timeline and distinguish completion rates from individual elapsed-time measures.

answer.text: Throughput.
answer.explanation: OS13 defines throughput as completed jobs divided by elapsed time. That exactly matches the stem’s process-completion rate. CPU utilization is busy-time fraction; response measures delay to first start, and turnaround delay to completion. The units therefore distinguish throughput from the other criteria without requiring a scheduling example.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU utilization measures busy-time fraction, not how many processes finish per unit time.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Response measures first-service delay for a process rather than a completion-count rate.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Throughput is explicitly the number of completed jobs divided by elapsed time.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Turnaround measures arrival-to-completion elapsed duration rather than completed jobs per time.

evidence.quote: For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B. With I/O, subtract all CPU and blocked time to isolate ready-queue waiting. Throughput=completed jobs/elapsed time; CPU utilization=busy time/elapsed time. Minimize response/turnaround/waiting under the selected goal and maximize useful throughput/utilization.

questions.stem: What does the Job Queue contain?

options.label: A
options.text: Only processes currently running on the CPU

options.label: B
options.text: All processes currently in the system, including those not yet admitted to memory

options.label: C
options.text: Only processes waiting for I/O devices

questions.hint: Decide whether the process is eligible, running or waiting, then identify the responsible queue or scheduling role.

answer.text: All processes in the broad textbook system/job-queue sense.
answer.explanation: OS06 explicitly defines the broad textbook job queue as processes in the system and distinguishes a narrower admission queue awaiting memory. B matches that broad usage, including not-yet-admitted jobs. Ready/running or I/O-blocked work are subsets, not the whole category; already-ended processes are not the intended current job population. The answer retains the note’s terminology qualification.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Currently running work is only a subset, not the broad population represented by the textbook job queue.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The broad textbook usage includes system processes/jobs, including those awaiting memory admission.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: I/O waiting belongs to device queues and does not exhaust the broad job-queue population.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Already-terminated work is not the current job population intended here’s broad system queue.

evidence.quote: The ready queue contains eligible work; device queues hold blocked requests. The broad textbook job queue contains processes in the system, while an admission queue more narrowly holds jobs awaiting memory/admission. Long-term scheduling admits jobs; medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work.

New processes are created/admitted; ready means eligible for CPU but not currently running. Running uses a CPU. Waiting/blocked means unable to proceed until an event; terminated means execution has ended. Running→ready follows time-slice expiry or another preemption. Running→waiting follows blocking I/O. I/O completion normally gives waiting→ready, not a guaranteed immediate running state.

questions.stem: In an open seekable file’s state, what does its current file-offset field (the file-position pointer, rather than the descriptor handle) track?

options.label: A
options.text: The physical location of the file on disk

options.label: B
options.text: The current position within an open file for the next read or write operation

questions.hint: Distinguish a file operation, a resource handle, an offset and file metadata.

answer.text: The current position within an open file for the next read or write operation
answer.explanation: The current offset records the logical position used for the next read or write on a seekable open file. A descriptor is instead a process-local integer handle referring to open-file state. Physical disk-block locations, permissions and creation timestamps describe other mapping or metadata information. By asking specifically about the position field, the revised stem makes B precise without conflating a descriptor with an offset.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Physical disk location is separate from the current logical I/O offset.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The file-offset field records the position for the next read or write.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Owner permissions are access-control metadata rather than the current position.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Creation time is metadata rather than the current I/O offset.

evidence.quote: A file has content and metadata such as name, size, owner, permissions and timestamps. open obtains an open-file reference, read/write transfer bytes, seek changes an offset, close releases a reference, truncate changes size and unlink removes a name. A file descriptor is a process-local integer handle; the associated open-file state contains the current offset and access mode. Descriptor and offset are not synonyms.
Read advances the offset on seekable files and may return fewer bytes than requested; zero normally indicates end-of-file.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of an Access Control List (ACL) in file protection?

options.label: B
options.text: To specify exactly which users/groups have which types of access (read, write, execute) to each file

questions.hint: Distinguish identity checks, permission checks and the particular security property at issue.

answer.text: Specify principals and permitted access rights.
answer.explanation: OS39 defines an ACL as listing principals and rights. B states that users/groups can receive different read/write/execute permissions for a file. Authentication verifies identity first; authorization uses these permitted operations. Space accounting, fragmentation and I/O ordering do not define an access-control list. The answer does not assume universal default rights or that every filesystem uses exactly the same permission model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Disk-space usage is storage accounting, not the list of principals and allowed operations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An ACL associates users/groups or other principals with specified access rights on the resource.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fragmentation concerns block placement and free-space layout rather than authorization entries.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Scheduling I/O requests controls service order, not which principal is authorized to access a file.

evidence.quote: Authentication verifies identity; authorization checks permitted operations. An ACL lists principals and rights; owner/group/other bits are a simpler policy model, not universal defaults granting all owners full access or everyone read. Read, write, execute, append and delete are different rights, with filesystem-specific rules.
Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit. External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation.
The ready queue contains eligible work; device queues hold blocked requests.

questions.stem: What is Contiguous Allocation of disk space?

options.label: A
options.text: Files are stored in scattered blocks linked by pointers

options.label: B
options.text: Each file occupies a continuous set of consecutive disk blocks, enabling fast sequential and direct access

options.label: C
options.text: Files are indexed using a separate index block

options.label: D
options.text: Files are allocated in fixed-size frames

questions.hint: Trace how logical file blocks reach physical blocks and account for pointer metadata.

answer.text: A file occupies consecutive disk blocks.
answer.explanation: OS38 defines contiguous allocation through consecutive blocks, with logical block i at start+i. This permits sequential and direct access without following a chain. B matches.
