Scattered pointers describe linked allocation, a separate index describes indexed allocation, and fixed physical memory frames belong to paging rather than file-contiguity organization. Growth and external fragmentation remain drawbacks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Scattered blocks linked by pointers describe linked allocation rather than one consecutive run.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A consecutive block run supports start-plus-index lookup and sequential/direct file access.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A separate block-pointer index describes indexed allocation, not contiguous placement itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Physical memory frames are paging units rather than the disk-block contiguity rule for a file.

evidence.quote: Contiguous allocation uses consecutive blocks; logical block i is start+i and supports direct access, but growth and external fragmentation are problems. Extents allow several contiguous runs. Linked allocation chains blocks and supports growth without reserving a complete contiguous file; locating block i requires traversing preceding links. FAT stores chains in a table; caching that table does not change the chain into a direct arithmetic mapping.
Indexed allocation uses a per-file array/tree of block pointers and supports direct lookup with metadata overhead.
Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P.

questions.stem: What problem does Linked Allocation solve compared to Contiguous Allocation?

options.label: B
options.text: It eliminates external fragmentation and pre-known file size requirements since blocks can be scattered and linked anywhere

options.label: D
options.text: It requires less memory for storing file metadata

questions.hint: Trace how logical file blocks reach physical blocks and account for pointer metadata.

answer.text: Linked blocks permit growth without reserving a full contiguous run.
answer.explanation: OS38 says linked allocation supports growth without reserving a complete contiguous file. Since successive blocks can occupy separate free locations, it removes the external-contiguity problem and the need to reserve the final length beforehand. B captures that advantage. Random access still requires traversing earlier links, internal last-block waste may remain, and no universal smaller-metadata claim follows.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Locating a later linked block requires traversal, so faster random access is not its general advantage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Separate linked blocks allow incremental growth without a single reserved contiguous region or preknown final length.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A partially used final block can still waste space internally; linking does not specifically remove that waste.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Pointers add metadata, and the note gives no universal less-memory guarantee over contiguous allocation.

evidence.quote: Contiguous allocation uses consecutive blocks; logical block i is start+i and supports direct access, but growth and external fragmentation are problems. Extents allow several contiguous runs. Linked allocation chains blocks and supports growth without reserving a complete contiguous file; locating block i requires traversing preceding links. FAT stores chains in a table; caching that table does not change the chain into a direct arithmetic mapping.
Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit. External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation.

questions.stem: In Indexed Allocation, what is the Index Block?

options.label: A
options.text: A pointer stored in each data block to the next block

options.label: B
options.text: A dedicated block containing all the disk-block addresses (pointers to data blocks) for a specific file

options.label: C
options.text: A table stored at the beginning of the disk for all files

options.label: D
options.text: A block that stores file metadata like size and timestamps

questions.hint: Trace how logical file blocks reach physical blocks and account for pointer metadata.

answer.text: A per-file block of data-block pointers in the simple indexed model.
answer.explanation: OS38 defines indexed allocation through a per-file array/tree of block pointers and gives an index-block capacity example. B describes the simple single-index-block form. Large files may need multiple index levels, so all addresses in one block is model-dependent rather than universal. A is linked allocation, C a global-table description, and D ordinary metadata without the defining data-block pointers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A next pointer in each data block describes linked allocation rather than a separate per-file index.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: In the simple indexed model, a dedicated per-file index contains pointers to the file’s data blocks.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A global table for all files is not the per-file index block described by indexed allocation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Size/timestamps alone do not provide the data-block address index that defines this allocation structure.

evidence.quote: Indexed allocation uses a per-file array/tree of block pointers and supports direct lookup with metadata overhead. A Unix inode can combine direct pointers with indirect levels. Check pointer size, block size, index capacity and whether metadata reads are cached.
A 1024-byte index block with 4-byte pointers holds 256 block addresses. With 1024-byte data blocks, one such index level addresses 256 KiB of file data, excluding metadata and any reserved entries.
FAT stores chains in a table; caching that table does not change the chain into a direct arithmetic mapping.

questions.stem: What is the difference between Sequential Access and Direct Access for files?

options.label: B
options.text: Sequential access reads/writes records in order; direct access allows jumping to any block/record position by specifying its block number

options.label: C
options.text: Direct access is only possible for text files

options.label: D
options.text: Sequential access requires more disk space

questions.hint: Trace how logical file blocks reach physical blocks and account for pointer metadata.

answer.text: Sequential access proceeds in order; direct access selects a position.
answer.explanation: OS38 contrasts linked traversal of preceding blocks with contiguous start+i and indexed direct lookup. These illustrate the access distinction in B: sequential progression versus selecting a numbered position without reading every preceding record. Nothing restricts direct access to text or requires sequential files to occupy more disk space merely because of their access method.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Order-dependent traversal and direct selection are different access behaviors, not identical methods.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sequential access advances through records; direct access identifies a chosen block/position for access.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The direct block-lookup rule does not impose a text-file-only restriction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Access order alone does not determine a greater storage-space requirement for sequential files.

evidence.quote: Contiguous allocation uses consecutive blocks; logical block i is start+i and supports direct access, but growth and external fragmentation are problems. Extents allow several contiguous runs. Linked allocation chains blocks and supports growth without reserving a complete contiguous file; locating block i requires traversing preceding links. FAT stores chains in a table; caching that table does not change the chain into a direct arithmetic mapping.
Indexed allocation uses a per-file array/tree of block pointers and supports direct lookup with metadata overhead.

questions.stem: What is a Tree-Structured Directory?

options.label: A
options.text: A directory where all files are in one flat list

options.label: B
options.text: A hierarchical directory organization with a root directory from which subdirectories and files branch out, each file having a unique path

options.label: C
options.text: A directory shared among multiple users

options.label: D
options.text: A temporary directory deleted on reboot

questions.hint: Follow namespace structure and distinguish names, underlying files and mounted filesystems.

answer.text: A rooted hierarchy of nested directories and files.
answer.explanation: OS37 says a tree allows nested directories and absolute/relative paths. In the pure tree model, each entry has a path from the root, matching B. Flat lists instead describe single-level organization; sharing among users and deletion at reboot do not define tree structure. Links can add graph relationships, but that is an extension beyond the pure tree premise.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: One flat file list is single-level organization rather than nested branches from a root.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A root with nested subdirectories and paths is the tree hierarchy described here.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiple users sharing a directory does not by itself define its structural hierarchy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Deletion on reboot is a lifetime policy rather than the rooted directory-tree organization.

evidence.quote: A single-level directory requires unique names in one namespace. Two-level directories separate users. A tree allows nested directories and absolute/relative paths; links can create shared graphs. Modern general-purpose systems commonly present hierarchical namespaces, but a feature name alone does not prove that every system excludes simpler arrangements.

questions.stem: What is the difference between Hard Links and Symbolic Links in file systems?

options.label: A
options.text: Hard links can span different file systems; symbolic links cannot

options.label: B
options.text: Hard links create multiple directory entries pointing to the same file's data blocks; symbolic links are special files containing the path to another file

options.label: D
options.text: Hard links are only supported in Windows

questions.hint: Follow namespace structure and distinguish names, underlying files and mounted filesystems.

answer.text: Hard links name one file object; symbolic links store a pathname.
answer.explanation: A hard link supplies another name for the same underlying file object; a symbolic link stores a pathname. Symbolic links can cross filesystems and may dangle, whereas ordinary hard links stay within a filesystem. Linux’s link operation supplies a direct counterexample to the Windows-only claim. unlink can remove a symbolic-link name, so the link is not undeletable. B states the correct distinction.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The boundary is reversed: symbolic links may cross filesystems, while ordinary hard links remain within one.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Both hard-link names identify the same underlying file; a symbolic link contains a pathname to resolve.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A symbolic-link name can be removed with unlink; removing it does not erase the target’s contents.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Linux provides hard links through link(), so they are not supported only in Windows.

evidence.quote: A hard link is another name for the same underlying file object, usually within one filesystem; a symbolic link stores a pathname and can point across filesystems or become dangling. Removing one hard link does not erase content while other names/open references retain it.

Linux provides link() to create another hard-link name for an existing file. The old and new names identify the same file, so hard links are not a Windows-only facility. unlink() removes a filesystem name; when that name is a symbolic link, it removes the link itself. Removing a name and erasing the target’s contents are different operations.

questions.stem: What is File System Mounting?

options.label: B
options.text: The process of attaching a file system to a specific location in the existing directory tree, making it accessible

options.label: C
options.text: Deleting old files to free disk space

questions.hint: Follow namespace structure and distinguish names, underlying files and mounted filesystems.

answer.text: Attach a filesystem at a mount point.
answer.explanation: OS37 explicitly defines mounting as attaching a filesystem at a mount point and distinguishes it from formatting. B states that integration into the existing namespace. Creation/formatting establish a filesystem’s on-device structure; deleting files frees content space. None of those is the namespace attachment operation requested by mounting.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Creating a new filesystem establishes storage structure rather than attaching it to an existing namespace.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Mounting makes a filesystem accessible at a chosen point in the directory hierarchy.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Deleting files changes contents/free space rather than attaching a filesystem to the namespace.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Formatting is explicitly distinguished from mounting in the supplied note.

evidence.quote: NFS provides remote filesystem access; FTP transfers files rather than itself mounting a local filesystem.
Disk initialization/filesystem creation is OS/tool work, firmware begins boot, and drive firmware may remap bad sectors.

questions.stem: In the context of deadlock recovery, what is 'Rollback'?

options.label: B
options.text: Returning a preempted process to a safe previous state after resources are taken back from it during deadlock resolution

options.label: C
options.text: Deleting all processes involved in a deadlock

options.label: D
options.text: Rebooting the computer to free all resources

questions.hint: Separate handling before allocation from actions taken after detection, and consider the cost of checking.

answer.text: Restore an affected process to a prior checkpoint after reclaiming resources.
answer.explanation: OS26 describes reclaiming safely preemptable resources and rolling affected work back to a checkpoint. B states that restoration to a safe prior state after resources are withdrawn. Restarting the entire OS/computer and killing all involved processes are different coarse recovery actions, not the meaning of rollback. Safe checkpoints/restart semantics are required to make withdrawal and restoration coherent.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Restarting the whole OS is not the checkpoint restoration of affected work that defines rollback.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Rollback restores an affected process to a previous recoverable state after safe resource reclamation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Terminating processes is a separate recovery tool rather than restoring their earlier execution state.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Rebooting frees broad machine state but is not the process-checkpoint restoration definition of rollback.

evidence.quote: Detection asks whether the current state is deadlocked. Recovery can terminate selected processes or reclaim safely preemptable resources and roll affected work back to a checkpoint. Termination and rollback are both possible recovery tools; choose according to the resource and process conditions.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of relocation/base and limit registers in the standard contiguous single-process-region memory model? The limit denotes the permitted region length.

options.label: A
options.text: They speed up CPU scheduling decisions

options.label: B
options.text: The relocation register stores the process’s physical base and the limit its permitted length; hardware checks the logical offset before adding the base

options.label: C
options.text: They track file system locations on disk

options.label: D
options.text: They manage virtual memory page tables

questions.hint: Apply the stated hole-selection or base-and-bound rule with its explicit convention.

answer.text: The relocation register stores the process’s physical base and the limit its permitted length; hardware checks the logical offset before adding the base
answer.explanation: In the standard base/limit model, the base identifies the process’s physical starting address and the limit gives its permitted length. Hardware checks that the logical offset is nonnegative and smaller than the limit, then computes base plus offset. This protects accesses to the assigned region. The registers do not describe the OS base and size, schedule CPU work, track disk files or manage page tables.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: These registers check memory accesses rather than schedule CPU work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The option states the process base, length bound and checked translation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Disk-block locations are not the purpose of RAM base/limit registers.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Simple contiguous base/limit translation does not manage page-table mappings.

evidence.quote: A contiguous allocation gives a process one continuous region. In the standard base/limit model, base is that process’s physical starting address and limit is its permitted length. Check 0≤logical_offset<limit, then physical=base+offset. The relocation register does not normally hold the OS base.
Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P. Divide virtual address v into page=floor(v/P) and offset=v mod P. The page table maps a page to a frame and protection/status flags.

questions.stem: In Dynamic Linking, what is a key advantage over Static Linking?

options.label: A
options.text: Programs run faster with dynamic linking

options.label: B
options.text: Multiple programs share one copy of library code in memory rather than each program embedding its own copy, saving memory

options.label: C
options.text: Dynamic linking eliminates the need for a page table

options.label: D
options.text: Dynamically linked programs cannot have bugs

questions.hint: Track when an address or library reference is resolved and the direction of translation.

answer.text: Share suitable library code pages across programs.
answer.explanation: OS27 says dynamic linking resolves external-library references at load/runtime and allows suitable library code pages to be shared, whereas static linking copies selected code into the executable. B captures the potential memory saving. It is not an unconditional speed guarantee, does not remove address translation/page tables and cannot eliminate programming bugs. Only shareable code/pages are implied, not arbitrary writable library state.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Dynamic resolution/sharing does not guarantee faster execution for every program or workload.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Several processes can share suitable library code pages rather than each embedding a separate static copy.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Library linking does not remove virtual-address translation or its page-table requirements.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Choosing dynamic rather than static linking cannot guarantee the absence of programming errors.

evidence.quote: Dynamic linking resolves references to external libraries at load/runtime, allowing suitable library code pages to be shared; static linking copies selected code into the executable.
Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P. Divide virtual address v into page=floor(v/P) and offset=v mod P. The page table maps a page to a frame and protection/status flags.

blocks.text: An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs.
Convenience means making tasks easy through consistent interfaces, files and device abstractions.
Efficiency means using resources effectively; it is not synonymous with the fastest response for every process.
Application development tools use OS services but application development itself is not a core resource-management function.
Ability to evolve means adding hardware support, features and repairs through maintainable interfaces/modules.
Backward compatibility preserves supported older application behavior; it is not a promise that every old binary works.
Scalability means handling greater workload/resources; portability means adapting to other platforms.
Fault tolerance continues correct service despite specified failures; recovery restores service afterward.
Updates and monitoring help administration, but automatic updates are not a defining property of every OS.
Operating System module
Oracle Solaris 11

notes.title: Batch, multiprogramming, time-sharing and real time

blocks.text: Batch jobs run with little interaction after submission.
Multiprogramming keeps several jobs available so another can use the CPU while one waits; it does not require fixed time slices.
Time-sharing uses rapid scheduling/preemption to support interactive users.
A single CPU interleaves execution; multiple CPUs can execute work truly in parallel.
Shared-memory multiprocessors do not require each CPU to have private main memory.
Single-user and multiuser describe concurrent user access, not the number of applications.
Network systems expose remote services; distributed systems coordinate work across machines, sometimes hiding location.
Real-time correctness includes timing: hard deadlines must be met, while soft deadline misses degrade service. “Real time” does not simply mean fast.
Spooling and multitasking are mechanisms, not proof of a particular OS generation.
Operating System module
The kernel implements core resource management, protection and system-call handling.
A shell reads/interprets user commands; a GUI is another interface.
Browsers, office tools and editors are applications.
Device drivers are commonly kernel components, although user-space drivers also exist.
Kernel mode has privileged operations; supervisor mode often means the same privileged mode, so offering both as exclusive answers is ambiguous.
Firmware/bootloader stages execute before transferring control to a kernel loaded into RAM.
The kernel is the first core OS component, not the first program ever executed at power-on.
Loadable modules can add drivers to a running kernel; “kernel modules cannot be loaded while running” is false in modular systems.
A resident kernel remains active through the session.
Utilities such as antivirus and disk tools can combine user processes with privileged components.
Operating System module
A system call requests a protected kernel service, such as creating a process, reading a file or opening a socket.
A user-facing API/library may wrap that request; not every library function enters the kernel.
Distinguish the application API from the direct user/kernel boundary when describing access to OS services.
Process control, file/device management, information retrieval and communication are service categories.
Video editing and a database-specific write_database() are application operations, not standard generic syscall categories/names.
Virtualization presents a virtual machine environment, often allowing guest operating systems on one host through a hypervisor.
It differs from virtual memory, which translates a process’s addresses.
Kernel, shell, API and VM are not interchangeable labels.
Operating System module
A program is stored instructions; a process is an executing instance with address space and resources.

A process does not universally “manage applications” or “provide a user interface.” The PCB records identity, state, PC/registers, scheduling information, memory/accounting details and I/O/open-resource state.
A saved PC identifies where execution resumes.
A context switch saves one execution context and restores another; useful application work is interrupted by this overhead.
An interrupt or system call can switch privilege without switching process.
Task is OS-specific terminology: it may mean process, thread or schedulable entity.
No universal process-versus-task distinction follows from the word alone.
Operating System module
New processes are created/admitted; ready means eligible for CPU but not currently running.
Running uses a CPU.
Waiting/blocked means unable to proceed until an event; terminated means execution has ended.
Running→ready follows time-slice expiry or another preemption.
Running→waiting follows blocking I/O. I/O completion normally gives waiting→ready, not a guaranteed immediate running state.
The ready queue contains eligible work; device queues hold blocked requests.
The broad textbook job queue contains processes in the system, while an admission queue more narrowly holds jobs awaiting memory/admission.
Long-term scheduling admits jobs; medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work.
The dispatcher performs the handoff/context restore after selection.
A bare “priority” causes running→ready only if a preemptive policy chooses another process.
Operating System module
UIC CPU Scheduling
Processes arise during initialization, user requests, service requests or a running process’s creation call.
In POSIX-style systems fork() creates a child: zero is returned in the child and the child PID in the parent on success.
The two have distinct address spaces, although resources may be shared through explicit mechanisms. exec replaces the current process image; it does not itself create another process.

Normal completion and a program-detected error exit are voluntary; an unrecoverable fault or being killed is involuntary. exit() terminates normally through the runtime; abort() requests abnormal termination.
A reference to nonexistent/protected memory is a fatal fault, unlike an application deciding to exit after bad input. “Terminate exit” is not a precise standard category.
Parent termination does not universally kill all descendants.
Linux man-pages fork(2)
Linux man-pages execve(2)
A thread has its own PC, registers and stack.
Threads in a process share code, address space and usually open-file resources.
A process can contain many threads; a thread belongs to one process at a time.
Threads are not a group of processes and need not execute sequentially.
Independent processes can exist; cooperating ones communicate/share data.
User-level threads are managed by a library; kernel threads are known to the OS.
In many-to-one mapping, a blocking kernel call can block all user threads and one kernel execution context cannot use multiple CPUs simultaneously.
One-to-one permits another kernel thread to run when one blocks.
Many-to-many multiplexes user threads over several kernel threads.
Speed and reliability depend on implementation; the management layer alone guarantees neither.
Application names such as browser or Excel do not prove a particular version’s threading model.
Operating System module
Shared memory lets processes access a common region and requires synchronization for conflicting updates.
Message passing exchanges data through send/receive operations.
Pipes provide streams; message queues preserve messages; sockets connect endpoints; RPC requests a remote operation.
HTTP is an application protocol over a communication mechanism and can carry interprocess communication, so it is not universally “not IPC.”
Blocking send waits for the required handoff/buffering/receipt condition defined by its API.
Blocking receive waits for a message.
Nonblocking operations return promptly with data, progress or a would-block result. “Sender blocked until received” identifies blocking send under rendezvous semantics.
File locks coordinate access rather than transfer arbitrary payloads, though locking is synchronization within IPC.
Do not equate asynchronous messaging with no synchronization ever.
Operating System module
A race occurs when results depend on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses.
A critical section is code accessing shared state that needs protection, not the resource itself.
A correct exclusion solution requires mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting under stated assumptions.
Mutual exclusion is a desired safety property; races, starvation and deadlock are possible failures.
Keep critical regions small and ensure every conflicting access uses the same protection.
A barrier waits until a defined set of participants reaches a point; a monitor encapsulates protected operations with condition synchronization.
Locking can itself introduce deadlock if acquisition order is inconsistent.
Worked microexample

items.text: Two threads read counter=0, each computes 1 and each stores 1. Two increments produce 1 instead of 2. Protecting the entire read-modify-write with one lock prevents that lost update.

blocks.text: Operating System module
A semaphore provides atomic wait/P/down and signal/V/up operations.
Under the nonnegative-token model, wait consumes one available token or blocks when none is available; signal supplies a token and may wake a waiter.
Implementations using negative internal counts encode waiters differently, so state the model.
A binary semaphore represents one permit; a counting semaphore tracks several.
A mutex normally has ownership rules that a general semaphore lacks.
Worked microexample

items.text: Initialize a mutex semaphore to 1. Each thread does wait(m); critical work; signal(m). For a buffer of N slots use empty=N, full=0 and mutex=1: producer waits empty then mutex, inserts, unlocks then signals full. Waiting for empty while already holding mutex can prevent the consumer from freeing a slot.

blocks.text: Arpaci-Dusseau and Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP Semaphores
Strict alternation uses turn=0/1: process i waits while turn≠i, then enters and sets turn to the other process on leaving.
It enforces turns but can violate progress if the other process stays outside its critical region.
A naive lock-variable test followed by a separate set races because both processes can observe free before either sets it.
Test-and-set and compare-and-swap combine checking/updating atomically; ordinary check-then-write does not.
Peterson’s classic algorithm uses flags plus turn for two processes under its memory-model assumptions; a semaphore can coordinate more than two.
Disabling local interrupts does not exclude other CPUs and is not a general user-space locking solution.
Interrupts can notify/synchronize events, so they cannot be universally excluded from every synchronization-related classification.
UIC Process Synchronization

For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B. With I/O, subtract all CPU and blocked time to isolate ready-queue waiting.
Throughput=completed jobs/elapsed time; CPU utilization=busy time/elapsed time.
Minimize response/turnaround/waiting under the selected goal and maximize useful throughput/utilization.
First construct a time line with arrivals, idle gaps, preemptions and overhead, then calculate per-process values before averages.
Do not confuse first response with final completion.
Worked microexample

items.text: A job arrives at 2, starts at 5, uses 4 CPU units without interruption and finishes at 9: response=3, turnaround=7, waiting=3. Six completions in two hours means throughput=3 jobs/hour.

blocks.text: Operating System module
Non-preemptive scheduling keeps a running CPU burst until completion, blocking or voluntary yielding.
Preemptive scheduling can return running work to ready, usually after a timer quantum or a more urgent arrival.
FCFS and non-preemptive SJF are non-preemptive; RR and SRTF are preemptive.
Priority can be either, so its name alone cannot decide.
Cooperative describes relying on voluntary release.
CPU preemption saves a context and reallocates processing time; taking an occupied printer or lock may be unsafe.
This is why time-slicing does not automatically remove the no-resource-preemption condition for deadlock.
Frequent switches have cost; non-preemptive policies can delay interactive work behind long bursts.
Operating System module
UIC CPU Scheduling
FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt.
If the CPU is idle, jump to the next arrival.
Long CPU-bound work can make many short jobs wait: the convoy effect.
A finite burst with finitely many jobs ahead eventually starts, but waiting can still be large.
FCFS does not universally have the worst turnaround for every possible workload.
Worked microexample

items.text: All ready at time 0, tie order P1=24,P2=3,P3=3: schedule 0–24 P1,24–27 P2,27–30 P3. Waiting times 0,24,27 average to 17. Turnarounds 24,27,30 average to 27. If arrivals are not simultaneous, recompute using their actual times.

blocks.text: Operating System module
Non-preemptive SJF/SJN chooses the shortest next burst among currently ready jobs.
SRTF reconsiders on arrivals and selects the shortest remaining work; a shorter newcomer can preempt.
Future burst lengths normally need estimates.

SJF minimizes average waiting for the usual fixed simultaneous ready set with known bursts and no preemption/switch cost; that theorem is not a workload-independent comparison against every preemptive policy.
Repeated short arrivals can starve a long job.
The shortest total original burst is not necessarily the shortest remaining burst after execution has begun.
Worked microexample

items.text: P1 arrives 0 with burst 8; P2 arrives 1 with burst 2. SRTF runs P1 0–1, P2 1–3, P1 3–10. P1 waiting=2 and P2 waiting=0. Non-preemptive SJF cannot interrupt P1 once it has started.

blocks.text: Operating System module
Priority scheduling chooses the highest-priority ready job.
Check whether a smaller or larger numeric value means higher priority.
State whether a high-priority arrival preempts.
Fixed-priority scheduling can starve low-priority jobs under continued high-priority load.
SJF can also starve long jobs; starvation is not exclusive to fixed-priority scheduling.
Aging increases waiting jobs’ effective priority according to a rule, reducing indefinite postponement when the priority scheme and workload permit.
It is not a deadlock cure.
Priority inversion occurs when urgent work waits on a resource held by lower-priority work; priority inheritance can temporarily raise the holder’s priority.
Operating System module

notes.title: Round Robin, quantum and bounded turns

blocks.text: RR serves a ready queue cyclically for at most quantum q per turn.
Unfinished jobs return to the tail; completed/blocked jobs leave.
Specify how arrivals at a quantum boundary enter the queue.
A large quantum approaches FCFS; tiny quanta increase switch overhead.
RR gives recurring opportunities, not identical total CPU consumption for jobs of different lengths.
With n continuously ready jobs, no priority bypass and zero overhead, a just-requeued job waits at most (n−1)q for its next turn.
This bounds one interval, not total lifetime waiting when arrivals or blocking are unrestricted.
Include context-switch costs if given.
Worked microexample

items.text: P1=5,P2=3, both arrive 0, q=2: P1 0–2,P2 2–4,P1 4–6,P2 6–7,P1 7–8. Completions 8,7; waiting=8−5=3 and 7−3=4; average 3.5.

blocks.text: Operating System module
A multilevel queue separates classes, such as foreground interactive and background batch, and chooses both between queues and within them.
Fixed interqueue priority may starve lower queues; allocating time shares between classes can avoid this.
A multilevel feedback queue allows movement according to observed behavior, commonly demoting CPU-intensive jobs and periodically boosting priority.
Do not infer movement from a simple multilevel-queue label.
State initial class, quantum per level, promotion/demotion rules and interqueue policy before tracing.
A binary search tree is a data structure that might implement a queue; it is not itself a CPU selection policy. “Infinite” is not a standard scheduling-policy category.
Operating System module
Fair-share scheduling allocates according to stated weights, potentially per user/group rather than per process.
Equal per-process RR can let a user obtain more aggregate CPU by launching more processes.
Proportional shares address that policy choice; fair need not mean equal.
Lottery scheduling assigns tickets and selects a winning ticket each turn.
With weights 3:1, expected shares are 75% and 25%; short-run results vary and this is not a deterministic no-starvation deadline.
Stride-style scheduling tracks progress toward shares deterministically.
Any “guaranteed scheduling” answer needs the actual guarantee and assumptions; finite FCFS and RR can also avoid indefinite postponement.
Worked microexample

items.text: If user A runs four ready tasks and B runs one, plain RR gives A about 80% overall. A policy granting each user half the CPU instead gives A’s tasks about 12.5% each and B’s task 50%.

blocks.text: Arpaci-Dusseau and Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP Proportional Share
Operating System module
There is no universally best policy for response, waiting, fairness and throughput simultaneously.
State the workload and objective, apply the algorithm and compare measured results.
Maximum waiting at submission is not determined from burst times alone if future arrivals, priorities or overhead are unconstrained.
Known finite workloads are different from an open stream with potential starvation.
An item asking for one non-preemptive algorithm while offering FCFS and SJN has multiple answers.
Equal share needs a process/user/group definition. “Highest average turnaround” requires a concrete workload; do not memorize FCFS as an absolute.
RR is a conventional interactive choice because turns improve responsiveness, subject to quantum and overhead.
Operating System module

notes.title: Deadlock and its four necessary conditions

blocks.text: A set is deadlocked when each member waits for an event/resource that only another blocked member can provide.
Mere waiting for another holder is normal blocking; indefinite unfair delay can be starvation without a cycle of dependencies.
Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource.
Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another.
No resource preemption means release must be voluntary.
Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.
All four are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model.
Their availability as general system policies does not prove a deadlock exists at this instant; inspect actual allocations/requests.
Preventing any one condition prevents that class of deadlock.
A preemptive CPU scheduler can coexist with deadlocked locks.
Worked microexample

items.text: P1 holds lock A and requests B; P2 holds B and requests A. Neither releases before acquiring the other: nonshareable locks, retained holdings, no forced release and a cycle all occur.

blocks.text: Operating System module
In a resource-allocation graph, P→R is a request and an instance R→P is an assignment.
Follow these directions to form waits.
No cycle implies no deadlock; with one instance of every resource type, a cycle implies deadlock.
With multiple instances a cycle alone is insufficient: another instance may permit completion.
A wait-for graph replaces single-instance resource nodes with P→Q when P waits for Q.
For a complete single-instance example, suppose P0 holds R0 and requests R1, while P1 holds R1 and requests R0.
The wait-for edges P0→P1 and P1→P0 form a cycle, so neither can proceed.
With multiple resource instances, inspect all assignments and available instances before concluding that a cycle is a deadlock.
Operating System module
Prevention constrains how requests are made.

Share a resource where safe to remove mutual exclusion; request all needed resources before holding any to remove hold-and-wait; permit safe resource withdrawal/restart to attack no-preemption; impose a global acquisition order to remove circular wait.
Not every physical resource is shareable or safely preemptable.
“If waiting, release all held resources and try again” removes simultaneous holding while waiting.
Distinguish voluntary resource release from forced preemption when describing resource reclamation.
Prevention can waste utilization or cause starvation; avoiding deadlock is not the same as treating every process fairly.
Operating System module

notes.title: Avoidance and the Banker safety test

blocks.text: Avoidance allows requests only if the resulting state remains safe.
Banker requires maximum claims.
Compute Need=Max−Allocation.
Set Work=Available and repeatedly find an unfinished process with Need≤Work componentwise; simulate completion by adding its Allocation to Work.
Finishing all gives a safe sequence.
Tentatively grant a request only if it is within Need and Available and the safety test succeeds.
Unsafe does not mean already deadlocked.
Banker is avoidance, not CPU scheduling, detection or prevention by breaking a condition.
Worked microexample

items.text: One resource type: Available=1; P1 holds 1 and needs 1 more; P2 holds 2 and needs 2 more. P1 can finish, returning its allocation so Work becomes 2; P2 can then finish. Safe order P1,P2. A maximum claim must be known before testing.

blocks.text: University of Illinois Chicago, Deadlocks
Detection asks whether the current state is deadlocked.
Recovery can terminate selected processes or reclaim safely preemptable resources and roll affected work back to a checkpoint.
Termination and rollback are both possible recovery tools; choose according to the resource and process conditions.
Repeatedly sacrificing the same victim can cause starvation.
Checking on every request versus periodically trades overhead against detection delay; no universal best interval exists.

Ignoring a sufficiently rare problem is sometimes called the ostrich policy, but real systems still prevent or detect selected deadlocks. “Deadlock acceptance” can mean intentional ignoring, not necessarily an invalid approach.
A detection graph, avoidance safety graph and ordinary scheduling queue solve different problems.
University of Illinois Chicago, Deadlocks

notes.title: Address binding, dynamic loading and linking

blocks.text: Compile-time binding uses absolute addresses if placement is known.
Load-time binding relocates when placed into memory.
Execution-time binding translates while running and permits movement with hardware support.
Logical/virtual addresses are generated for a process; physical addresses select RAM.
An MMU translates logical addresses to physical addresses, not the reverse.
Dynamic loading brings a routine in when needed.
Dynamic linking resolves references to external libraries at load/runtime, allowing suitable library code pages to be shared; static linking copies selected code into the executable.
Swapping traditionally moves a whole process to backing store; paging moves individual pages.
These differ from a context switch, which primarily changes execution state.
Operating System module
A contiguous allocation gives a process one continuous region.
In the standard base/limit model, base is that process’s physical starting address and limit is its permitted length.
Check 0≤logical_offset<limit, then physical=base+offset.
The relocation register does not normally hold the OS base.
If limit instead means last valid offset, the inequality changes; specify the convention.
First-fit selects the first adequate hole; next-fit continues from the previous search position; best-fit selects the smallest adequate hole; worst-fit selects the largest.
No policy universally optimizes both search time and future storage utilization.
Binary-fit is not one of these standard names.
Worked microexample

items.text: Holes 100,500,200,300 and request 180: first-fit selects 500, best-fit 200, worst-fit 500. For base=4000,length=100, logical offset 99 maps to 4099; offset 100 traps.

blocks.text: Operating System module
Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit.
External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation.
Coalescing joins adjacent free holes; compaction moves allocated regions to consolidate free space and requires relocation support.
Basic fixed-frame paging avoids external fragmentation of page-frame allocation but can waste the final page internally.
Variable-length segmentation/contiguous partitions can fragment externally.
This is not a statement that every allocator inside a paging OS is fragmentation-free.
Track units and round allocations up rather than assuming all requests exactly fill blocks.
Worked microexample

items.text: A 10 KiB object in 4 KiB pages needs ceil(10/4)=3 pages: 12 KiB allocated and 2 KiB unused. Two 3 KiB free holes cannot serve one contiguous 5 KiB request although 6 KiB is free.

blocks.text: Operating System module
Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P. Divide virtual address v into page=floor(v/P) and offset=v mod P. The page table maps a page to a frame and protection/status flags.
Physical address=frame×P+offset.
A TLB caches translations; a TLB miss may require a table walk while the page is already resident.
Table size depends on the number of virtual pages and entry size, not just physical RAM.
Protection and present bits must be checked before access.
A page-table lookup is not a CPU scheduling operation.
Worked microexample

items.text: Page size 1024, v=2053: page 2, offset 5. If page 2 maps to frame 7, physical address=7173. With 16-bit virtual addresses and 1 KiB pages, there are 64 virtual pages and a 6-bit page number.

blocks.text: Operating System module
Segmentation uses logical variable-length units such as code, stack and arrays.
A segment-table entry provides base, limit and permissions.
For (segment,offset), validate the segment and check the bound, then add base+offset.
An out-of-range offset traps; it must not spill into the next segment.
Under the basic models, paging uses fixed units/page tables and can waste space internally; segmentation uses variable logical units/segment tables and can fragment externally.
Segments reflect program structure whereas ordinary pages are largely transparent to applications.
Apply all three contrasts when comparing paging and segmentation.
Worked microexample

items.text: Segment 1 has base 8000 and length 500. Offset 120 maps to 8120; offset 500 is invalid under the length convention.

blocks.text: Operating System module
Virtual memory provides translated, protected address spaces and allows nonresident portions of a program to be backed by storage.
It does not add physical RAM or remove all capacity constraints.
Demand paging brings a page in when accessed.
On a nonresident access: trap, validate mapping/permissions, find a frame or choose a victim, save a dirty victim if needed, obtain contents, update mapping and restart.
Not every fault reads a disk: some allocate zero-filled pages or establish shared mappings.
An illegal access is rejected, not automatically loaded.
Excessive active-page demand can cause thrashing: repeated faults dominate useful computation.
Reducing active load or adding suitable memory can help.
Worked microexample

items.text: If access costs 100 ns and an additional page-in costs 5 ms, a fault probability of 10^−4 adds roughly 500 ns per access; rare long delays still matter.

blocks.text: Operating System module
Replacement chooses a victim when no suitable free frame is available.
FIFO evicts the earliest loaded page; a hit does not refresh insertion time.
LRU evicts the least recently accessed and updates recency on every access.
Optimal evicts the page used farthest in the future, serving as an offline lower bound.
LFU uses reference counts and needs tie/aging rules.
Write a row per reference, identify hits before evicting, and count initial loads as faults.
FIFO may exhibit Belady’s anomaly when more frames cause more faults; LRU and optimal have the stack property.
Page buffering retains useful free/modified pages to reduce effective fault cost.

notes.title: Device controllers, drivers and I/O services

blocks.text: A controller is device hardware exposing status, control and data registers.
A driver converts OS requests into device-specific operations.
Device independence and uniform naming hide brand-specific details; error handling reports/retries supported failures.
Polling checks readiness repeatedly; interrupts request CPU attention; DMA transfers blocks after setup without CPU work for every byte.
Both the kernel and drivers participate in I/O; specify the abstraction level being discussed.
Plug-and-play discovers/configures compatible new hardware but may still require a driver.
Input/output/storage/NIC devices are OS-managed hardware; user accounts are identities.
Printer-paper and network errors can be handled/reported, but continued operation during total power loss requires hardware support, not OS software alone.

Buffering temporarily holds data in transit to absorb speed/transfer-size differences.
Caching retains copies to accelerate reuse.
Spooling queues jobs for a device such as a printer, usually on disk, so producers need not own it throughout job creation.
These have different purposes even if one implementation combines them.
The clock/timer supports timekeeping, timeouts, accounting and preemptive scheduling.
A system monitor reports CPU, memory, storage and network usage; it measures rather than directly creating more resources.
Disk initialization/filesystem creation is OS/tool work, firmware begins boot, and drive firmware may remap bad sectors.
A broad “OS does all disk functions” claim needs these responsibility boundaries.

A file has content and metadata such as name, size, owner, permissions and timestamps. open obtains an open-file reference, read/write transfer bytes, seek changes an offset, close releases a reference, truncate changes size and unlink removes a name.
A file descriptor is a process-local integer handle; the associated open-file state contains the current offset and access mode.
Descriptor and offset are not synonyms.
Read advances the offset on seekable files and may return fewer bytes than requested; zero normally indicates end-of-file.

Sockets also support ordinary read/write, alongside socket/connect/send operations, so read is not uniquely “not a network call.” FAT32, NTFS and ext4 are filesystem formats; HTTP is an application communication protocol.

A single-level directory requires unique names in one namespace.
Two-level directories separate users.
A tree allows nested directories and absolute/relative paths; links can create shared graphs.
Modern general-purpose systems commonly present hierarchical namespaces, but a feature name alone does not prove that every system excludes simpler arrangements.
A hard link is another name for the same underlying file object, usually within one filesystem; a symbolic link stores a pathname and can point across filesystems or become dangling.
Removing one hard link does not erase content while other names/open references retain it.
Mounting attaches a filesystem at a mount point; it does not format the device.
NFS provides remote filesystem access; FTP transfers files rather than itself mounting a local filesystem.

notes.title: Contiguous, linked and indexed file allocation

blocks.text: Contiguous allocation uses consecutive blocks; logical block i is start+i and supports direct access, but growth and external fragmentation are problems.
Extents allow several contiguous runs.
Linked allocation chains blocks and supports growth without reserving a complete contiguous file; locating block i requires traversing preceding links.
FAT stores chains in a table; caching that table does not change the chain into a direct arithmetic mapping.
Indexed allocation uses a per-file array/tree of block pointers and supports direct lookup with metadata overhead.
A Unix inode can combine direct pointers with indirect levels.
Check pointer size, block size, index capacity and whether metadata reads are cached.
Worked microexample

items.text: A 1024-byte index block with 4-byte pointers holds 256 block addresses. With 1024-byte data blocks, one such index level addresses 256 KiB of file data, excluding metadata and any reserved entries.

Authentication verifies identity; authorization checks permitted operations.
An ACL lists principals and rights; owner/group/other bits are a simpler policy model, not universal defaults granting all owners full access or everyone read.
Read, write, execute, append and delete are different rights, with filesystem-specific rules.
Least privilege limits damage.
Password hashing verifies secrets without storing plaintext; one-time passwords expire after use.
Encryption protects confidentiality under correct key use but does not automatically provide integrity.
Trojans masquerade as useful software, worms propagate independently and viruses attach to hosts; denial of service harms availability.
Modern OS families can support cryptography, authentication and firewalls, but support/configuration depends on product.
CLI, GUI, speech/natural language and VR are possible interfaces, not a closed list excluding the last two.

Linux is a Unix-compatible kernel written from scratch by Linus Torvalds; a distribution combines it with userland, libraries and tools.
Android’s base kernel layer is Linux; its framework and applications are higher layers.
AOSP is open source, while a shipped device can include proprietary applications/services.
Windows and macOS are both proprietary products, although macOS contains open-source components, so “which is not open source?” offering both is ambiguous.
Microsoft Office is an application suite.

notes.title: UNIX origins and the first four historical generations

blocks.text: UNIX development began at Bell Labs in 1969, led by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie with other collaborators. Ritchie is therefore a co-creator, not the sole inventor of the first operating system.

The later UNIX time-sharing system described by Ritchie and Thompson is multiuser and interactive and supports asynchronous processes. Its later versions incorporated multiprogramming. This history does not make UNIX the first system ever to multitask.

In the first four generations of the cited NYU teaching taxonomy, the first generation uses vacuum tubes and manual single-user operation without a separate resident OS. The second generation pairs transistors with uniprogrammed batch systems; the resident OS starts successive jobs without being reloaded for every job.

The third generation pairs integrated circuits with multiprogramming. The fourth emphasizes personal computers. These are characteristic-era associations, not claims that each feature existed exclusively in one era.

notes.title: Thread management costs and execution privilege

blocks.text: In the conventional library-thread comparison, user-level thread creation and switching can avoid entering the kernel. Kernel-managed thread creation and management commonly incur additional kernel work and are therefore generally slower to create and manage in this comparison. This is a typical comparison, not a universal speed or reliability guarantee.

Being scheduled or managed by the kernel does not give application thread code kernel privilege. Ordinary applications and supporting utilities execute in restricted user mode and request protected services through libraries and system calls. Kernel component code executes in privileged kernel mode and performs permitted low-level hardware operations.

Operating System module · page 29

Memory management tracks which primary-memory regions are free or in use, assigns memory to processes and data, and deallocates it when no longer needed or when a process terminates. Allocation and deallocation concern memory ownership; CPU selection belongs to scheduling.

A buddy allocator manages power-of-two block sizes. It takes a smallest sufficient block, splitting larger blocks when necessary, and can merge a freed block with its free buddy. This is not the worst-fit rule of selecting the largest arbitrary hole.

A fetch policy decides when contents are brought into memory; demand paging fetches a valid nonresident page when it is accessed. A cleaning policy concerns writing modified contents to backing storage. A replacement policy chooses which resident page to evict. These decisions can cooperate during one page fault, but they are different decisions.

notes.title: Communication endpoints and timed I/O events

blocks.text: In the descriptor-based socket API, socket() creates a communication endpoint and returns its descriptor. connect() associates the socket with the requested peer address; send() transmits data to another socket. Receiving through read() uses the ordinary descriptor-input interface described in the file-services lesson.

IRQ means interrupt request. A controller can raise an interrupt to request CPU attention. In a clock-tick scheduler, the scheduler initializes a running process’s quantum counter; each clock interrupt decrements it, and reaching zero triggers scheduling. Clock support also maintains time of day and usage accounting.

Direct message communication names the receiving process explicitly. Indirect communication uses a mailbox or port. This naming distinction is independent of whether a send or receive blocks: naming a destination does not determine synchronization semantics.

A compiler translates source code toward an executable representation. For example, the conventional GCC toolchain distinguishes preprocessing, compilation proper, assembly and linking. A compiler uses operating-system services as a development tool; it is not the runtime kernel component that selects ready processes, manages memory or handles protected service requests.

Linux provides link() to create another hard-link name for an existing file. The old and new names identify the same file, so hard links are not a Windows-only facility. unlink() removes a filesystem name; when that name is a symbolic link, it removes the link itself. Removing a name and erasing the target’s contents are different operations.

note_intro.text: An OS controls resource sharing, protects programs and provides convenient services. Learn the state changes and algorithms behind each term. Scheduling and deadlock questions require explicit assumptions; a policy name alone does not establish a universal performance ranking.
Draw process-state transitions and a Gantt chart before calculating scheduling metrics. Record arrivals, burst lengths, priority convention, quantum and switch cost.
For deadlock, identify held resources and directed waits; distinguish prevention, avoidance, detection and recovery. CPU preemption is not the same as resource preemption.
